cells.tense: You are standing inside a clarity that has only just begun to arrive.
cells.act: go all the way into the pattern until you meet its edge
cells.ask: Take the rent split, or the weekly schedule, and go deeper into it than your usual stopping point. Read the whole shape twice, slowly, dull stretch included, until you find where it ends. Keep it inside the reading; say nothing.
cells.core:
Something here weighs out even, and you can tell most days. The cut of clarity has arrived without wrecking anything: you can hold a thing as it stands and still move. When you size up what's around you, the proportions come close to right, and the sizing doesn't eat you.

The next depth is yours. Take an arrangement you've stood over many times and go further in than the old stopping point. Not to worry it — to find its edge. Every shape has one, and the ones worth knowing hide theirs further in than you'd guess. Reaching it teaches you something, and your sense of proportion stays steady afterward.

cells.tense: You have already decided what this feeling means before it has fully arrived.
cells.act: let what was only possible stand finished
cells.ask: Carry one half-made thing through to the end it actually has — into the form it's already taking, not the finished version you keep rehearsing. When it lands where it lands, stop there.
cells.core:
Where you look, you're measuring before the picture is finished. Your eye keeps correcting ahead of itself — this one will land badly, that one is heading somewhere worse — and the corrections are getting more accurate than anything in the frame. You're right often enough that each hit feels like balance, and this is what one sees when certainty has outrun contact.

What's out of proportion is the correcting, not the eye. So carry what was only possible to its full size, on one thing, today: bring the half-made thing into the form it actually has, no bracing, no rehearsing how it lands. Finish it because you began it. Knowing how the sentence turns out before you finish it is a strong skill, and it belongs to what's here, not to the next one.

cells.tense: The clear look was possible and it did not happen then.
cells.act: bring the directed work to its full standing
cells.ask: Go back to one piece of work that went quiet and bring it up to standing — a payment given a date, a time pinned into an agreement. Once it holds, leave it.
cells.core:
Something got set aside and the picking back up stopped, and you've quit expecting it. You can look at what's around you without anything closing the loop: the eye is fine, it just isn't being used for anything, and it knows the difference. It's more that the weighing went quiet than that you chose to sit down.

What's starved is the part of you that looks and then moves. So bring one directed thing to full standing — a schedule written where you'll see it, a payment set to leave on a fixed date, a time pinned into an agreement. Making it stand does the work, not looking. Don't push yourself to be moved by it afterward. A thing held up a month without your hand tells you something about your weight in it.

cells.tense: The turning is happening and you are talking about the weather around it.
cells.act: meet what is arriving as it arrives
cells.ask: As the next message, person, or feeling comes in, say to yourself what it is, plainly, before you carry on. Let it be met while it's new, without a verdict attached.
cells.core:
You met something recently, and the meeting is already closed in the telling. Someone asks how the day is and you say fine, and the thing entering gets left out of the account. It isn't hidden — you just don't call it a turning when it turns. The eye that catches it is working; the telling strips the catching out.

Something is arriving now, in this place, whether it gets named or not. Say the next one as it comes — not the past and not the meaning of it — and make that the whole of what you do with it. This isn't a decision about the arrival, or a story about the arrival; it's one sentence about what just walked in, kept that small. Then release it. Enough for a week, done a few times, at the size it actually happens.
